items.question: What If Europe colonized the Americas four centuries earlier? 1092 Instead of 1492
human_answers: Lots of feedback and responses! Thank you all! I'll get to responding to other replies later on. The Crusades! That's a good point for the year 1092 and the 11th century. Also lots of good points here. Very good points. Crusader-style polities and principalities in the New World, given the attitudes of the 11th century. 1. Why wouldn't a less-weakened Muslim power establish their own colonies? As long as they're in Iberia or Morocco, they got a good chance of colonization with that geography, I think? 2. Also why not? What if the Apache or some other First Nations group taking over the North American interior, like a counterpart to the Mongols. Hopefully less bad and deadly and painful though, though that's probably too much to ask for when it comes to warfare in general. "What if the Americas were colonized by Europe beginning in 1292?" Could be worth it's own thread! Here in this one we're talking about what if 1092 instead of 1292, or OTL 1492.

That's a fun scenario to consider. One way to get Medieval America... Not sure about the naval tech of the time though. Or the ressources given the voyage between Europe and the Americas are going to be months long. These are the two crucial things that need to be fixed to get the possibility. The North Route via Greenland and Vinland probably is the best shot to make this work. Think the issue is the fact the Atlantic Ocean is pretty devoid of islands that can make effective island-hoping stops. There are the islands of Macaronesia (Azores, Canarias, Madeira, Cape Verde) close to Europe but otherwise it's a long trip until you reach the Carribeans or one of the American coasts. This isn't the same situation as the Pacific where you have tons of small islets... unless you go into ASB territory and raise the Azore plateau but that basically is making Atlantis a real thing... Naturally this situation limits the abilities of Muslim powers to colonize. Europeans at least have the Viking routes, even if that requires a successful Vinland. Though one has to remember the legend of Abu Bakr II of Mali, the most likely fictionnal predecessor of Mansa Musa. It's a stretch and we're more dealing with an African power than a European or Arabo-Muslim one, but the distance between West Africa and Brazil is a lot shorter... But then again, it's basing ourselves on a myth.

As for how would see a medieval colonization of the Americas, I would expect it happened across the Northern Atlantic and would likely focus first on the region around St Lawrence Bay, which offer several good settlements, than we would see it spread up the St, Lawrence River and later down the East Coast. Early settlements would simply be normal Norse settlements, and outside Norse settlers the main early source of “settlers” would be slaves. The need for labor would drive this slave trade and the victims of this slave trade would likely mainly come from the British islands, the Baltics, Central Europe and the post Frankish kingdoms in order of importance and it would likely disappear by the 13th century. The early settlements would likely mostly be peasants republics, as the Norse seems to mostly have established those on the frontiers. Over time we will likely see consolidation of power under large land owners both secular and ecclesia and the rise of city states. Also as the Norse runs into more powerful native societies, we may also see more centralized frontier states lead by Norse war leaders, these may also turn on the less centralized Norse states and begin to establish true kingdoms. As the population we also see the arrival of Low German merchants, who establish merchant quarters in the cities, we will likely see German artisans also moving. We could also see something like the Ashkenazi migration to Poland, but it’s more likely that Low Germans simply will fill that niche as they did in the Baltic and Nordic countries. This may result in the rise Low German city states. At the same time the Catholic Church will likely introduce more warm weather crops as the Norse moves south. As the economy of Norse America grows and expand, others will likely look into establish alternative trade route to it. Here we may see the Portuguese doing their own Columbus expedition in the early 15 century. At that point I would expect a European presence already in the Caribbean, even if it’s not fully developed. So the Portuguese establish trade routes to the Caribbean and introduce Mediterranean and Middle Eastern cash crops. We likely also see the rise off the African slave trade, but with greater European and Mestizo presence in the region already, it likely doesn’t reach OTL levels and the more traditional European structure likely means a more serfdom like structure for the African slaves. I suspect the Norse will run into the Mesoamericans in the 14th century and we will see it falling to Norse invaders or crusaders, with it being relative far away from Norse American strongholds (which will likely be the Mississippi and St. Lawrence basins and the East Coast), I expect the model of conquest will be more like the Baltic crusades. Conquest mostly by knightly monastic orders and Mexico under a knightly Grandmaster. We could easily see a repeat in the Andeans, but we could also just instead see Christian missionaries converting them.

I am not familiar with the shipbuilding industry, but I believe this is possible. There was no fundamental difference like scale or materials between shipbuilding in the 15th and 11th century. They likely needed only to devise a few new designs, or simply undertake bold try using the vessels they already have. As for the difference? An 11th-century conquest of the Americas would have been far more likely to result merely in the emergence of independent states, rather than colonies subservient to Old World powers. At best, the Italian city-states might have established a few small commercial colonies (perhaps in the Caribbean region?), but inland colonies dominating an entire continent would have been highly unlikely. This aligns more closely with the norms of that era, and the comparatively weaker commercial and artisanal capabilities of Europe would not have generated the centripetal force required to establish such a relationship; Europe could not produce so many goods that American colonists were unable to manufacture for themselves. Two rather interesting questions: 1. Could a less weakened Iberian/North African Muslim power have established its own colonies in the Americas? 2. Could a nomadic polity have been established in the North American interior?

The major issue is that open ocean travel isn't really possible before the 15th century so you'd be island hopping like the Norse did. That's certainly possible but your probably looking at a more Polynesian or Greek heroic age style model (or for that matter the Norse in Iceland and Greenland) where people are leaving to found a separate colony rather than one controlled from the Metro-pole as its to far away. Also most of the early arrivals will be in the North (Canada, then moving into New England and points south as the Little Ice age bites) and while trade webs will probably see the European diseases spread there is a good chance the native powers will have time to recover before actual Europeans reach them. That could allow the Mexican civilizations and the Inca a good chance to survive especially if they've obtained European tech in trade before the newcomers have the forces to go after them (the Aztec are probably doomed whatever as the events of OTL strongly suggest they were hated by all and someone was taking them out eventually). Also its likely they understand pretty quickly this is a new land and not a route to China (or at least not an easy one, especially once they finally sight the great desert of the Plains prairie and realize just how big America really is) so there will probably be a much stronger focus on going south to round Africa to reach the Spice islands. With actual transoceanic travel developed much earlier (and the need to improve links with the New World driving sailing tech along at a fair clip) that's likely to see Portugal starting its investigations long before Spain is finished with the Reconquista and probably with England and France nipping at her heels this time. An early rediscovery (or more dissemination of the original Norse discovery) probably doesn't completely prevent the Crusades (there is still the issue of Jerusalem) but with a bigger target for expansion and as an outlet for violence the majority of settlers will probably go there rather than the rather precarious Outremer and even if the First Crusade succeeds it may not establish an enduring polity (they had enough trouble getting immigrants as it was. Usually Europeans only went East when the states were in deep trouble). Although with a Europe that has an outlet for its expansionist desires in the Far West and doesn't feel so under siege for the first time in centuries might be able to patch things up with Islam a bit more easily. Hard to say about Religion although by 1092 the Great Schism has already happened so the Catholics will be very much the first ones there and its hard to say if there will even be a Reformation after four centuries of altered history. However if the Crusades are averted, or at least blunted there is a good chance Byzantium survives in its original form and without the damage from the Latin occupation it might be able to hold out and reform enough that they can avoid falling to the Ottoman's. Also Venice and the Italian city states may not rise as quickly if the focus on trade switches to the Atlantic (especially if the wealth of America is discovered).

items.model_answer:
If sustained European colonization of the Americas had begun around 1092 instead of 1492, the world would probably look dramatically different, but not in a simple “everything happens 400 years earlier” way. The biggest constraint is that Europe in 1092 was much less capable of overseas empire than Europe in 1492. So the most likely outcome is not an immediate Spanish-style conquest of entire continents, but a slower, patchier, more fragile Atlantic world that reshapes both hemispheres over centuries.

In 1092, western Europe was politically fragmented, economically weaker, technologically less advanced in navigation and shipbuilding, and much less able to project sustained power across an ocean. There were precedents for long-distance Atlantic travel, especially the Norse in Greenland and Vinland, so contact is not impossible at all. But building a stable colonial system would have required regular shipping, military reinforcement, agricultural adaptation, and administrative organization that most European kingdoms of the late eleventh century struggled to sustain even close to home. So colonization beginning in 1092 would probably start from the North Atlantic fringe—Norse Greenlanders, perhaps followed later by English, Breton, Norman, or Iberian ventures—rather than with immediate penetration into the Caribbean, Mexico, and Peru.

Even so, the most transformative effect would still likely be disease. If Europeans established repeated contact centuries earlier, Eurasian pathogens would reach Indigenous American populations much sooner. That would likely trigger demographic collapse in many regions long before the rise of the Aztec and Inca empires in the forms we know from the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. This is one of the biggest consequences of the altered timeline: many famous states encountered by Columbus, Cortés, and Pizarro might either never emerge, emerge in different forms, or be much weaker by the time stronger European monarchies eventually became involved. Earlier disease shocks could destabilize urban centers, political authority, tribute systems, and trade networks across the Americas over a long period rather than in one compressed sixteenth-century catastrophe.

That in turn means later medieval and early modern Europeans might encounter a hemisphere already transformed by centuries of intermittent contact, epidemic disruption, and selective exchange. Some Indigenous societies would collapse, but others would adapt, migrate, consolidate, or militarize. You might see new hybrid coastal polities arise, especially in the northeast of North America or around accessible Atlantic zones, combining Native political structures with imported animals, metals, and perhaps Christianity. Since the contact begins earlier and more gradually, there is a greater chance of mixed societies emerging before large centralized conquest states are feasible.

Europe itself would also be changed, though not necessarily enriched overnight. Earlier access to American crops could be enormous in the long run. If maize, potatoes, beans, squash, and possibly tomatoes moved into Europe centuries earlier, medieval agriculture and population growth might accelerate. The potato especially, if widely adopted, could eventually support denser populations in northern Europe much sooner. But adoption would not be immediate; medieval societies were conservative, transport networks limited, and agronomic knowledge poor. So the Columbian Exchange would still take time. Even so, an earlier transfer of crops could strengthen Europe demographically before the early modern era and perhaps soften some later famines.

There would probably also be major effects on Africa and the Islamic world. If Atlantic colonization begins in the late eleventh or twelfth century, Atlantic commerce may develop earlier, potentially reducing the centrality of some Mediterranean routes over time. That could alter the balance between Latin Christendom and the Muslim polities controlling key Eurasian trade corridors. On the other hand, because medieval Europe lacked the naval and financial machinery of later empires, the Atlantic might remain a secondary frontier for a long time. The Crusading era could blend ideologically with transatlantic expansion, giving colonization a more overtly religious and frontier character than the crown-directed mercantile imperialism of the sixteenth century.

One crucial uncertainty is labor. In actual history, large-scale plantation slavery in the Americas developed in the context of early modern capitalism, sugar expansion, and maturing Atlantic state systems. In 1092, those systems did not yet exist. So even if colonization began, it might not immediately generate the same plantation complex. Serf-like labor systems, raiding, tributary arrangements, and small settler colonies are more plausible early on. But over centuries, if profitable Atlantic crops emerged and maritime capacity improved, an earlier version of the transatlantic slave trade could eventually develop—possibly beginning sooner than in real history, though perhaps in a more decentralized and irregular form.

Politically, earlier access to American wealth might help certain European states centralize sooner. If Iberian kingdoms, Norman rulers, or even Angevin and later English monarchs gained profitable overseas footholds, that could alter state formation in Europe. But there is also a paradox: because eleventh- and twelfth-century rulers were weak, overseas colonies might become semi-independent lordships rather than tightly controlled royal possessions. The Americas could first be colonized more like crusader states, trading enclaves, marcher lordships, and monastic settlements than bureaucratic empires.

For Indigenous Americans, the timeline is mixed but overall disastrous in broad demographic terms. Earlier contact means earlier epidemics, violence, displacement, missionary pressure, and ecological disruption. Horses, cattle, pigs, iron tools, and new crops would spread earlier too, which could empower some societies and revolutionize transport, warfare, and agriculture centuries ahead of schedule. Plains horse cultures, for example, could arise much earlier if horses escaped or were traded inland. But the general pattern would still favor the hemisphere connected to the larger Afro-Eurasian disease pool and metalworking tradition. The result is likely not Indigenous preservation through earlier warning, but a longer period of upheaval.

By 1492 in this alternate world, the Atlantic is probably not being “discovered” by Columbus at all. Instead, it may already be a known, if still dangerous, zone of intermittent trade, fishing, raiding, missionary work, and settlement. European maps might include parts of northeastern North America, Greenland-linked routes, perhaps some Caribbean or mid-Atlantic islands if they had been reached. The great sixteenth-century conquests might either happen earlier in some form or, more likely, happen differently because the Americas would no longer contain the same political and demographic landscape.

In the very long term, global integration probably happens earlier, but more unevenly. Europe may gain food crops, land, and strategic depth sooner, potentially making it stronger earlier relative to other Old World powers. items.question: What If an earlier, more thorough modernization of Russia
human_answers: I would highly recommend you watch NojRant's NOT the Origins of Russian Authoritarianism . If you'd like a forum post, read my posts in another thread from here onward to here : they briefly go over parts of what you're interested in, and some of it is repeated below. If you want good detail, I'd recommend Robert K. Massie's book Peter the Great . tl;dr - clothes were only a small part of the reforms, there was major modernization of the economy, education and the legal system, and you seem to have a very, very stereotyped and caricaturish understanding of the topic to speak with such confidence. The problem with the reforms was not in their superficiality, but that most of them required follow-through by Peter's successors that, for reasons I'll get into, did not happen until Catherine II some 40 years later. A highly ideological statement if ever I've heard one. Define what it means to be 'European' in clear terms. Absolutism is actually a major benefit in this situation, mainly because it is not a parliament. Parliament is essentially a tool for the ruling class to give themselves endless privileges and benefits: a ruling class composed of rural nobility would see urbanization as a threat to their power over their tenants (and ultimately their wealth) and pursue policies that deurbanize the country, whereas one dominated by bourgeois interests would be enriched by urbanization. Urbanization ultimately leads to a richer, stronger, more industrialized nation overall, while deurbanization does not. As long as Russia has a strong nobility and a comparatively weak bourgeoisie, parliament is a nonstarter for your purposes because the default net effect of parliamentary actions will be to increase nobles' control over their tenants, hence limiting urbanization, hence limiting development of private capital for industrialization. A country with no strong king to keep the nobility in check will increasingly resemble basketcases like high medieval Hungary or early modern Poland, where the nobility could ignore the king as they pleased and even fight each other as warlords ( picrel ). Even in a lesser form, this can have severe consequences: for example, under the Dual Monarchy, the Hungarian half of the empire was granted wide-ranging autonomy, which the Magyar nobility used to systematically and shortsightedly block the development of industry. The result was that Hungary remained agrarian and economically backward, even failing to compete in agriculture - the thing the Magyar nobles had sought to protect - to the extent that Russian grain imported via the Adriatic was undercutting Hungarian grain on the Austrian market. In a strong monarchy, even if the king still has to appease the nobility somewhat, he has control over the spigot of privileges and benefits and only gives them out when he has to, and expects loyal service in return - and can even retract privileges if his position is strong enough, like Ivan the Terrible did in Russia or Charles XI did in Sweden (ref. the Great Reduction ). This is constitutionally impossible with a strong parliament, though the king can always try his luck with a coup or a civil war. Even strong monarchs who retained parliaments as vestigial organs of the state, like Louis XIV, actively avoided involving them in political decisions because they knew that weak parliaments were made strong by getting involved in decisions that could've been made by the king's bureaucrats instead. However, monarchies can be weakened by unexpected deaths, child kings / regencies, changes in dynasty, coups, successful riots by the urban population against taxes, and successful rebellions by uppity nobles. These events force the king to repeal unpopular laws and grant new privileges to the nobles in exchange for their support, because his normal ability to make himself obeyed by his subjects is drastically reduced and he needs to sweeten the pot for them to obey him again. This must be avoided to preserve the king's power and prevent the nobility from pressuring him to grant more privileges. 17th century Russian tsars were weakened by the Time of Troubles, which allowed the nobility to demand a host of new concessions in exchange for their support of Mikhail Romanov as the next tsar. The most notable concession was that their pomestie fiefdoms, which were previously non-hereditary and granted to them in exchange for service to the state, were made hereditary. Russian tsars spent the next century trying to repeal these various privileges with limited success, and were occasionally hampered by new setbacks, such as the 1648 salt riot , which led to tighter restrictions on serfs being introduced to satisfy the nobility. 18th century Russian tsars were weakened by chronic succession problems, which resulted in the new tsar/tsarina having to bribe the nobility as a class with extra privileges to get them to accept their rule. The reason was that Peter had revised the succession law from male primogeniture to "Whoever the tsar chooses," meaning that the tsar's will could be forged or denied by any member of the imperial family who could bribe the palace guards to support them in a coup. Catherine I, Elizabeth, Catherine II and Alexander I all rose to the throne this way. Doable - NojRants covers this succinctly in the Serfdom section of his video. If you can't avoid the Time of Troubles, then you need to avoid all further destabilizing events which allowed the nobility to wring additional concessions out of the tsar. If you want participation in European scientific exchange, look to the Russian Academy of Sciences. Its alumni included such giants as Lomonosov: they corresponded regularly with their peers in the rest of Europe, and many foreign luminaries visited to teach at the academy, such as Euler. Many advances in cartography, botany and geology came from the work of scientists who had been educated in the Academy or invited from abroad to work there. But given the list of names you chose, I suppose your chief interest in the Enlightenment is politics. Of which I frankly don't see the point. If you want to be welcomed at the salons of Paris and London, dressing in European fashion is a bonus, otherwise you might taken as a neat little foreign curiosity. What led you to this conclusion?

I would like to see that properly thought out! ... but: You'd probably need to address the "modernisation challenge" that any Eastern European polity would face and that stems from the divergent socio-economic foundations on which society rested in Western and Eastern Europe respectively. This hearkens back to the Middle Ages and the long-term demographic consequences of the Mongol devastations and the division of labour that only became more and more entrenched over the centuries: The High Middle Ages saw a trend towards slow re-urbanisation, communalism, development of crafts, revitalisation of trade, a new surge in scholarship and education, and while the epicentres of this were in Italy, France, along the Rhine and across the channel in England, this was, in the 11th and 12th centuries, a trend that spread everywhere, towards the North and towards the East. Kiev was a huge bustling urban centre of trade, learning... I know that the "Mongol explanation" is criticised for being overused in the history of Eastern Europe. But the Mongols did wipe out particularly the urban populations and, where their influence lingered, continued to be an important indirect factor working against urban communal independence, hemming the kind of social milieu from which early modern advances stemmed. And so, even before the conquest of the Americas by Western European powers, Eastern Europe became tendentially focused on exporting unprocessed raw materials while Western Europe developed proto-capitalist structures and more and more complex structures of value addition - and while the latter fomented the growth of a bourgeoisie, the latter could do with mostly just landowners and peasants. This is the situation you're still facing in a 17th century Russia, and every new world crop that was invented and massively increased agricultural productivity in Russia would, under these circumstances, only deepen the continental division of labour. The basic difference between Dutch society and Russian society was not clothes, you are right, but it also wasn't some political or religious agenda of its individual rulers. It was, I would argue, that the Netherlands had a sizable and growing bourgeois class where ideas which we consider "modern" grew and were pushed, while Russia had much less of that. Thus, in my eyes, the real challenge you're faced with is how to close or bridge this gap of bourgeois development.

This is more thinking aloud on possible developments that you'd need than dismissing this as impossible, but "the modernization didn't go deep enough" raises the question on what would be enough. Russia is rather removed from being comparable in some significant ways to England and France even in Ivan's (as in Ivan the Terrible) time for a multitude of reasons, and that's with quite a bit longer than a POD in Fyodor III's time. You'd probably need something where there's more capital (and that going into trade and industry) for Russia to meaningfully resemble the West in the sense you're aiming for, which is not something any tsar can simply make from sheer determination and energy or Peter would have managed it OTL. Saying this was OTL too much focused on clothing and beards is being rather unfair when he genuinely wanted a stronger and richer Russia and was trying to make one, not just imititate Western European fashions. I'm not saying someone else couldn't have done better than him (I'm very sure someone more familiar with economics than I can describe his failings much better than this post), but anyone in this position has a lot of work ahead of them.

Actually, modernization did start almost immediately after the ToT. However, it is rather difficult to expect some kind of a miracle from a poor country with very limited natural resources surrounded by the aggressive enemies. So obviously the progress was slow and not because of the Dutch clothing. The beards considerably shortened during Alexey’s reign and by time of FIII death the Hungarian dress became popular. FIII conducted a fundamental administrative reform when he abolished appointments by the pedigree. Formally, it was: the imperial status was recognized throughout Europe and after the GNW it became a dominating regional piwer. Serfdom in a form everybody is talking about only started during the reign of PI and reached its apogee during the “enlightened” reign of CII. BTW, a “popular perception” among the noble classes, merchants and manufacturers by the time of CII was that serfdom is beneficent for economy. How and why would it change? AFAIK, since mid-XVII the “enlightened absolutism” was a trade mark in what you are calling “Europe” (geographically, Russia was the biggest European country). Now, this is a truly interesting part. Can you please elaborate on how exactly it will get richer within social and economic framework reasonably well related to OTL? This is a genuine question and a meaningful answer will be greatly appreciated. How Enlightenment improved life of the French lower classes in the XVIII century? Well, some of these “giants” had been simply bought (reasonably cheap) by CII, which guaranteed acceptance of the Russian aristocrats in the salons Paris as welcomed equals regardless of their intellectual capacities. I’m sure that in London’s and Paris’ equivalents of the saloons they were even more welcomed. BTW, by mid-late 1700 Russia had a reasonably well developed literature. Unfortunately, Russian drama of that time was, as in the rest of Europe, under the French influence (eek) but this did not apply to the comedies. This is quite possible by the virtue of him not being Peter and a chance to avoid the GNW. However, the problem of the natural resources will not go away and neither would one of the fools and roads.

If Russia had modernized earlier and more thoroughly—especially in the 18th or early 19th century—the biggest likely result is that it would have become a more stable, competitive great power with fewer of the violent ruptures that defined its modern history. But that depends on what “modernization” includes. If it means not just military reform and industrialization, but also stronger legal institutions, broader education, administrative competence, infrastructure, and some gradual political reform, then the consequences could have been enormous.

Economically, earlier modernization would likely have reduced Russia’s long-term backwardness relative to Western Europe. One of imperial Russia’s core problems was uneven development: pockets of advanced industry existed alongside massive rural poverty and social stagnation. If serfdom had been abolished earlier, agriculture reformed more effectively, and transport and industry developed sooner, Russia might have built a larger internal market and a healthier middle class. That would have strengthened state finances, improved productivity, and made the empire less dependent on coercion to maintain order.

Socially, the most important effect might have been to weaken the extreme tensions that later fueled revolution. Russia entered the 20th century with a huge peasantry, harsh inequalities, weak civil institutions, and an autocracy that resisted meaningful power-sharing. Earlier modernization could have created more channels for social mobility and political participation. That would not necessarily have made Russia a liberal democracy, but it might have made it more reformable and less vulnerable to collapse under pressure.

Politically, this is where the counterfactual becomes most significant. A more modern Russia with stronger institutions might have avoided the 1917 revolutions, or at least made a Bolshevik seizure of power far less likely. If the tsarist state had evolved into something closer to a constitutional monarchy or a more bureaucratically capable authoritarian state, it may have survived the stresses of war and industrial change. That would have altered not just Russian history but world history: no Soviet Union in its actual form, no Stalinist terror on the same scale, and a very different ideological struggle in the 20th century.

In military and geopolitical terms, an earlier-modernized Russia might have performed better in key conflicts such as the Crimean War, the Russo-Japanese War, and even World War I. Better logistics, industry, education, and command structures could have made Russia far more formidable. A stronger Russian Empire might have had greater influence in Europe, Central Asia, and East Asia. That could have changed alliance systems and possibly the timing or nature of major wars. At the same time, a more capable Russia might also have been more expansionist, so modernization would not automatically mean a more peaceful Europe.

There are limits to the scenario, though. Russia faced serious structural obstacles: vast distances, harsh climate in many regions, low population density in some areas, ethnic and religious diversity, entrenched aristocratic interests, and a political culture built around centralized autocracy. Modernization would have threatened powerful groups, especially landowners and court elites. So “earlier modernization” would have required not just enlightened rulers but sustained political will and administrative capacity over generations. That is a very demanding condition.

It is also possible that partial modernization could have made things worse in the short term. In many societies, modernization destabilizes old systems before new institutions are ready. Expanding literacy, urbanization, and industry can produce stronger opposition movements if political reform lags behind. Russia actually experienced some of this. So if modernization had been economic and military but not political and social, the empire might still have faced upheaval—possibly even earlier.

Overall, the most plausible answer is that a genuinely earlier and broader modernization of Russia could have produced a stronger state, a more productive economy, and a less explosive society, making revolution and totalitarianism less likely. The modern world would then have looked very different. items.question: What If Britain and France made peace in 1811?
human_answers: I definitely agree that the conflict in Spain would continue, and that some form of renewed conflict in Europe down the line is inevitable, but I don’t think Napoleon wouldn’t try to conclude a peace with Britain, so long as it was on terms favourable to him. Now, whether that is possible is a rather different question. The Whigs at least had no interest in continuing to fund the peninsular war regardless, but in negotiations, they are likely to push for a restoration of Portugal and Hannover, and for France to at least withdraw from direct control of the rest of the Hanseatic cities and the Netherlands. It’s quite a lot for Napoleon to be willing to give up, though could possibly be paired with his longstanding designs on Sicily and a British withdrawal from Malta, as well as the return of occupied Dutch and French colonies. Regardless, I don’t think the British could get everything they want.

No mention has been made of the Continental System. I presume it is abolished as part of the peace treaty. And Britain's blockade is lifted. Anything less makes peace a non starter. Predictions from here: Overall peace is going to be short lived. Every one will be watching France waiting for a propitious moment to reduce the almost total hegemony France has. Nap will maintain a large military to enforce his hegemony. I don't know that this is sustainable. Spain will remain a bleeding ulcer. The Spanish people will continue to resist. Nap's best chance at lasting peace is to pull out and return a Bourbon to power. Remaining in a constant state of this kind of war drains resources, but brings no benefits. The best he can hope for (remaining in the conflict) is an uneasy truce where Joseph is somewhat accepted/propped up, while a low level of guerilla warfare continues. The entire Spanish colonial sphere is lost even faster than OTL. Cuba/puerto rico might remain attached, but I doubt it. I don't know whether Britain has destroyed Spain's infrastructure yet, but if not, Spain could actually emerge from the conflict in better shape without Britain's help than with it. Portugal might be able to hold out behind the line of T, as their soldiers have been trained up to a better level than before 1807, but as the British had supplied the top chain of command, they'll be left rudderless. I think their fate lies in how much stomach Nap has for continuing his Iberian adventure. It would be interesting to see what results if Nap simply walks away. OTL, the British acted as a regency while the Braganza court remained in Brazil. Joao did not want to return. Pedro was too young. Portugal is likely to be chaos. Should France manage to take control, Portugal itself may end up in better shape, but the entirety of the colonial sphere attaches to Brazil. I don't think the return of French colonies does much for France. Haiti is finished as a rich colony. Martinique and Guadeloupe, where Britain ironically enforced the status quo maintaining the slave system after capturing the islands, might still hold value. When the Nap Wars resume, Britain faces a hard choice - join in and try to reset the balance of power, or stay on the sidelines and have the European dynamic dictated to them. If they join in, they're quickly going to regret dropping out in the first place. They had France on the ropes in Portugal/Spain, and now they'll have to start all over again. Who knows what has become of Wellington.

The default of the Revolution certainly left its mark, but Napoleon was also ideologically opposed to debt, in part because of fiscal conservatism (there was a hyperinflation crisis during the Revolution), but also because it would have meant making himself dependent on the financial market, and he feared that the banker would try to exert political pressure on him. But I don't think he necessarily tried to raise a large amount of debt from the public market, he preferred to use a sinking fund controlled by one of his appointees for that. For the reparation, he had ways to force the issue, like sending his army in and making the host pay for its quartering. This was the way he was making his puppets, like the Kingdom of Italy, contribute, and alongside their allied contingent, it saved him as much money as the reparations brought him. For Prussia specifically, they were raising a large debt to pay the reparation, with Napoleon himself being one of their creditors, so they probably intended to pay. But you also have to take into account that Napoleon did not hesitate too much to raise taxes (he essentially brought back every indirect tax of the Ancien Régime) or defer payment, after the Restoration, the Bourbons had to pay the equivalent of one year of fiscal revenues in unpaid expenses.
items.original_question: What if Britain and France made peace in 1811? In 1810 King George III suffered a mental breakdown, and in early 1811, his son the Prince of Wales, later to reign as King George IV, was installed as regent by Parliament. The Prince Regent was widely expected to dismiss Spencer Percival’s government, and appoint Lord Grenville as Prime Minister, but was dissuaded from this course by his mother. Unlike the Tories, Grenville and the Whigs were sceptical of the conflict with France, particularly the expense of maintaining Wellington’s army in the Peninsula War, and had they taken power in 1811, whilst Wellesley’s army was holed up behind the lines of Torres Vedras, attempts at negotiating a peace with France are not an unrealistic prospect. Negotiations in 1807 touted an exchange of Sicily for Hannover, and Britain would retain the Cape Colony and Malta, whilst returning other Dutch and French colonial possessions, though these ultimately broke down over Sicily. Talks in 1808 even saw Napoleon offer to concede both Hannover and Portugal, though there is some question of how serious both sides were in this later negotiation. Both of these were also viewed by the Tory governments as a chance for a respite alike to Amiens, rather than to conclude the conflict. The Whigs, less intractable towards the idea of a French dominated Europe would be willing to pursue a long term peace. In addition to questions over Portugal, Hannover and the colonies though, France had by this point annexed the Netherlands and the Hanseatic cities, both of which are likely to be sticking points for British negotiators (although these annexations were in part to enforce the continental system). What terms could realistically be feasibly agreed by both sides at this time? With the end of the war with Britain in 1811, Napoleon’s invasion of Russia appears unlikely to my mind, though relations between the two emperors would undoubtedly continue to deteriorate. The peace would also presumably be unpopular domestically in Britain, where support for the war remained high. Austria, Prussia and Sweden all additionally had cause to want revenge against France and Napoleon, and so it seems unlikely that this peace would be entirely conclusive, and some form of renewed conflict seems eventually likely, even if it only comes with Bonaparte’s death. The aftermath of Amiens however suggests that this might well come sooner. There is however also the question of whether France could afford to maintain their precarious financial situation, and in particular continue to field their army without the subsides of allies, the reparations of former enemies and loot. It seems unlikely France can afford to demobilise in the face of their European rivals, so would this possibly prompt further campaigns? Perhaps against Russia regardless or the Ottomans?

items.model_answer:
If Britain and France had made peace in 1811, the Napoleonic era would probably have ended very differently: not in a dramatic military collapse of Napoleon, but in a negotiated European order dominated by a still-powerful French Empire. The most important consequence is that peace in 1811 would have removed the main source of pressure that kept the wider anti-French coalition alive. Britain was Napoleon’s richest, most persistent enemy. If London and Paris had settled their conflict, the wars on the Continent would likely have slowed, and some of the events that actually destroyed Napoleon—especially the invasion of Russia and the great coalition war of 1813–1814—might never have happened, or would have happened in a much weaker form.

The first major effect would have been economic and maritime. By 1811, both powers were exhausted by long war. Britain was straining under trade disruption, high debt, and political pressure from merchants; France was struggling to enforce the Continental System and alienating much of Europe in the process. A peace settlement would likely have involved Britain recognizing much of Napoleon’s European settlement, while France would abandon hopes of defeating Britain through commercial blockade. Britain would remain the dominant naval and colonial power. It probably would keep most of the overseas gains it had made, because that was where its bargaining strength lay. France, in turn, would keep its core continental empire and the political influence it had established over much of western and central Europe. In other words, the likely compromise is British supremacy at sea and French supremacy on land.

That alone would have transformed European politics. In the real timeline, Britain subsidized resistance to Napoleon across the Continent and kept pressure on him in Spain and Portugal. If peace came in 1811, British financial and military support for the Peninsular War would likely end or sharply diminish. That matters enormously. The Peninsular War was one of Napoleon’s greatest drains on men, money, and prestige. Without British armies under Wellington operating in Iberia, French control in Spain would probably remain troubled, but it would be far more sustainable. Guerrilla resistance would continue, but Spain would be less likely to become the open wound that it was historically. Portugal might be forced into accommodation with France or left in a neutralized position under British guarantee. Either way, Napoleon would no longer be bleeding strength there on the same scale.

The Russian question is crucial. Napoleon’s invasion of Russia in 1812 came in large part out of the breakdown of his continental system and his rivalry with Tsar Alexander I. If Britain and France made peace in 1811, one of the central causes of Franco-Russian tension would weaken immediately, because the continental blockade against British trade would lose much of its purpose. That does not mean France and Russia would become friends. Their rivalry over Poland, eastern Europe, and prestige would remain. But Napoleon would have much less reason to launch the catastrophic invasion of 1812, and Alexander would have less reason to posture as Europe’s liberator against French domination. A cold peace or limited confrontation becomes more likely than the vast war that actually wrecked the Grande Armée.

If Napoleon avoids the Russian disaster, his regime becomes much more durable. In 1811 he was still at the height of his power. His armies had not yet been broken, and his legitimacy had recently been strengthened by his marriage into the Austrian imperial family and the birth of an heir. A peace with Britain at that moment could have frozen Europe in a Napoleonic shape for years, perhaps decades. The Confederation of the Rhine, the Duchy of Warsaw, the Kingdom of Italy, and satellite monarchies in Spain, Naples, and elsewhere might have persisted, though not all equally securely. Austria and Prussia, both weakened and cautious after earlier defeats, would probably have accepted the settlement at least for a time. They might resent it, but without British money and without a French disaster in Russia, they would be far less likely to risk another major war.

This does not mean Europe would become stable in a modern sense. Napoleon’s empire had deep structural weaknesses. It depended heavily on military prestige, family rule, coerced alliances, and constant intervention. Nationalist resentment in Germany, Spain, and elsewhere would still exist. French domination of Europe would remain unpopular. Over time, any serious succession crisis, economic downturn, or major diplomatic quarrel could reopen the conflict. But the timing would change. Instead of Napoleon falling in 1814–1815, he might survive much longer and die on the throne, leaving his son a chance—however uncertain—to inherit a Bonapartist continental bloc.

Britain, meanwhile, would likely emerge richer and more commercially secure in the medium term. Freed from the immense cost of continental war, it could concentrate on trade, empire, and naval policing. The end of war would also change domestic politics. There might be less immediate pressure for military spending, less justification for wartime repression, and perhaps faster reintegration into global commerce. But Britain would also have to accept a Europe closed off politically by French influence. It would remain safe from invasion and globally powerful, yet strategically frustrated by French dominance from the Channel to the Oder.

The biggest long-term implication is that the nineteenth century might lose its familiar post-1815 settlement. No Congress of Vienna in the same form, no Bourbon restoration in France, no Waterloo as the symbolic end of the revolutionary and Napoleonic age. The conservative international order associated with Metternich and Castlereagh would be much weaker or delayed. Liberalism and nationalism might spread in a different pattern, because Napoleonic institutions—legal reform, secularization, administrative centralization—would remain embedded across much of Europe under French sponsorship rather than surviving as the mixed legacy of a defeated conqueror. Germany and Italy might still unify later, but under very different pressures and perhaps against a longer-lasting French hegemony.

So the clearest answer is this: peace in 1811 would most likely have preserved Napoleon’s empire rather than destroyed it. Britain would keep the seas and its colonies; France would keep most of continental Europe. The Peninsular War would shrink, the invasion of Russia might never happen, and the coalition that eventually overthrew Napoleon would probably fail to form. Europe would become a negotiated bipolar system—British maritime empire and French continental empire—at least for a generation, with later conflict likely but no longer certain to end in Napoleon’s rapid collapse.

human_answers: I can easily see Quebec not wanting to be part of either France, or USA. So they'll opt for independence. France never really wanted it back, so they won't get into their own American Revolution. Even if they did, it is the cost that will impact the French Revolution. The cost will add to French woes. This notion that France will rise up in revolution because Quebec wants independence is erroneous. France wanted regime/gov't change, which is not at all what Quebec wants (independence). France will add Quebec to the list of grievances. That does NOT make Quebec the birthplace of this alt FR. There were various causes of the ARW. One of them was putting Ohio under Canadian jurisdiction. Plus the French and Indian War was fought over the Ohio Valley, and led to a lot of the grievances leading to ARW. No one considers Ohio the birthplace of the AR. Semantics? maybe, but I don't think so.

It is difficult to ascertain how the French in Canada felt, as they lived in a quasi-medieval subsistence economy. Although not under full-blown feudalism, their society was paternalistic, hierarchical, and agrarian. The Church and the seigneurs (many of the seigneuries were owned by religious orders) were the pillars of authority. This is crucial in explaining the lack of widespread revolutionary fervour. However, in the late eighteenth century, there remained a cultural and sentimental connection to France, particularly to the Ancien Régime and the monarchy. After the executions of Louis XVI and Marie Antoinette, masses were said for them, and the French press in Quebec noted this. They were mourning the grandson of their last French sovereign, not celebrating the secular republic that executed him. In December 1778, from Boston, French Admiral d’Estaing called on the Canadiens to rise and rejoin their motherland, but this was difficult as Canada was where most British forces were stationed. It is unclear whether they wished to return to France, but the Continental Congress felt uneasy about the French returning to North America. Because the Canadiens were largely illiterate (literacy was still below 40% in 1850), it is difficult to say whether they were politically sophisticated, as the colony had been largely marginal and lacked a large merchant class under French rule. Education was not widespread and was largely controlled by seminaries or convents. It was even less politically sophisticated than the Spanish colonies in the Americas. My guess is that independence would have been the least likely of options, unless the Bishop of Quebec assumed the role of head of government.

Then the place will find a way to get out of American control ASAP. Mismatched expectations and all that because of a fundamental misreading by the Continental Army/Congress of the situation, particularly WRT the Quebec Act. The French never wanted to retain Canada après la Conquête because the sugar colonies in the Caribbean were far more valuable, plus lots of bad blood between the Canadiens and Versailles about which direction their part of New France should go. You'd basically be accelerating the French Revolution's TL but with a Canadien cause - and this time the British would come off as the good guys by allying with the habitants, whether or not it takes it back under its wing or accepts it as an independent country but under the British sphere of influence. And it finds a way to get out of the US ASAP, particularly if the initial military occupation goes as OTL and they basically alienated everyone. More probable than getting annexed by the US. Considering Quebec in this case would be a direct cause for the French Revolution ITTL, that's easy to remark on. While still predominantly Francophone (albeit with Canadian French given the same recognition as, say, Brazilian Portuguese), society and culture would take a more, say, Argentine or Uruguayan-like direction but w/ its own quirks (including probably far more indigenous influence) and probably different relationships among groups that would be relatively more egalitarian and opposed to reinstating the colonial relationship. Considering the British would still be next door viz. Newfoundland and Nova Scotia, as well as the HBC doing its thing, British influence would remain strong and that would include the cultural sphere, too.

If the Americans can't keep the Iroquois mostly neutral, and if they prevent them from trading with the Canadiens, then Quebec will want want to leave in a hurry. If the Americans could be deft in the administration of Quebec, better in battle, luckier with allied victories, and more skillful in peace negotiation I think there is a good chance that the Canadiens would want to be in a confederacy, or a customs union with a mutual defense pact. So those populations would have thrown a new political impulse into the country later especially after the Constitution is ratified.

items.original_question: What if Americans capture Quebec in 1775. How does Quebec's culture & society develop? So having just watched a new video from Blue, it gave me an idea of dusting off an old topic I used to talk about In 1775, the Continental Army under Generals, Richard Montgomery, Daniel Morgan, James Livingston, and Benedict Arnold (Yes, that Benedict Arnold) marched north into Canada in an attempt to capture Quebec from the British and persuade the French Canadians in joining the revolution. It went well for part of the expedition at first, with Montgomery nearly capturing British Govenor Guy Carleton in Montreal. Meanwhile Arnold's part journeyed through the wilderness to get to Quebec City, which was very difficult. However, by the time the Americans gotten to Quebec, a snowstorm occurred and the battle turned into an utter disaster. Montgomery got killed, Arnold was wounded, smallpox plagued the Americans, the British suffered few causalities, and the Americans managed to alienate the Canadians. Meanwhile, Carleton received reinforcements and made a counter offensive that drove the Americans back to Fort Ticonderoga. For context, what if the Americans captured Quebec? Say Montgomery captured Govenor Guy Carleton and the Americans managed to catch Quebec City by surprise. In my previous thread about the fate of Quebec (Roughly around Lower Canada; Upper Canada is a whole other can of worms), there were four possibilities I gave, but we're going to talk about three: A) French route- The Americans offer Quebec back to France for support in their war, meaning France regains Quebec by the end of the war B) American route- The Americans annex Quebec, making Quebec part of the USA. C) Independent route- The Americans make Quebec into a sister republic, making Quebec independent by the end of the war. (There's no British route since that OTL) Now, I want to focus on one particular aspect of the fate of Quebec: Culture. If Quebec wasn't under the British/TTL Canada, what would culture be like for the French Canadians. Depending on the route we take, how would culture, society, art, cuisine, fashion, etc, develop for the French Canadians? In the French route, how would Quebec be affected by the French Revolution? In the American route, how would Quebec develop under the USA? In the Independent route, how would Quebec develop stuck between the British and Americans while having access to the St Lawrence?

If the Americans had captured Quebec in 1775 and held it, Quebec would probably still have remained overwhelmingly French-speaking and Catholic for a long time, but its political identity would have developed very differently. Instead of becoming the core of a British Canadian state, it would have been folded into the revolutionary world of the United States. That would not mean rapid assimilation into Anglo-America, though. In the late eighteenth century the American rebels were not in a strong position to replace Quebec’s population, religion, or legal customs overnight, and they would have had good reasons to conciliate the French Canadian majority.

The first big issue would have been religion and law. One of the main reasons the Continental Congress tried to win over Quebec in the first place was by promising liberties rather than forced cultural change. If the Americans had succeeded, they likely would have had to preserve Catholic worship, tolerate the Church, and probably leave much of French civil law and seigneurial landholding in place, at least temporarily. Otherwise they would have faced constant resistance from a population that was already wary of both British and American Protestants. So in the short run, Quebec might have resembled a more northern version of later Louisiana: politically attached to the United States, but socially and legally distinct.

That said, integration into the United States would still have changed Quebec’s trajectory in major ways. The American Revolution and the political culture that followed were less accepting of corporate privileges, aristocratic hierarchy, and established church influence than either old France or the British imperial settlement in Quebec. Over time, American state-building would likely have weakened the seigneurial system earlier, reduced the political power of the Catholic clergy, and promoted elected institutions more aggressively. Quebec society might therefore have become more republican and locally political earlier than it did under British rule, but not necessarily more culturally English at first.

Language would be the central long-term question. Under British Canada, French survived in large part because Quebec became the demographic and institutional center of French Canada. If Quebec became part of the United States, French would probably remain dominant locally for decades, especially in the countryside and parish life, but it would face stronger pressure from English over the nineteenth century. Migration from New England and New York into the St. Lawrence valley would likely be heavier than in actual history, especially after independence and westward expansion stabilized. American commercial networks, courts, newspapers, and politics would reward English. French would survive, but probably in a more regionally confined and defensive way, rather than as the language of a future province leading a bilingual federation.

This means Quebec’s culture might evolve into something like a large-scale northern analogue of Cajun or Creole Louisiana, though more populous and therefore more resilient. French Canadian identity would still exist, but perhaps less as the basis for a quasi-national project and more as an ethnic, regional, and religious identity inside the United States. Instead of becoming one of the “founding peoples” of Canada, French speakers in Quebec might become one of several major American minority cultures. Their institutions—schools, churches, local courts, presses—could still be substantial, but they would likely have to fight harder to preserve them against pressures for linguistic and civic standardization.

There is also the question of slavery, race, and continental politics. If Quebec joined the United States early, it would almost certainly enter as a free or gradually freeing region, since slavery there was limited and the climate and economy did not favor plantation development. That would place it in the northern political orbit. In the nineteenth century, a French Catholic Quebec inside the United States might become associated with northern anti-slavery politics, immigrant Catholic politics, and resistance to nativist Protestant movements. Its Catholics would likely face the same anti-Catholic suspicion that Irish and other Catholic groups later encountered, but because Quebec’s population was older, rooted, and regionally concentrated, it could respond with stronger local solidarity.

The biggest difference from real history is that there would probably be no Confederation in the form we know it, and no Quebec as the principal French-speaking province within Canada. Without British Quebec anchoring a northern empire, the rest of British North America might fragment, shrink, or reorganize around the Maritimes and the far interior. That matters because real Quebec’s culture was preserved not only by local stubbornness but by its constitutional place in Canada. Inside the United States, Quebec would lack that same kind of guaranteed national bargaining position. It might still keep its language and faith, but with less formal protection and more dependence on local majorities and state rights.

So the most likely outcome is not that Quebec becomes instantly “Americanized,” nor that it remains unchanged. Rather, it becomes a French-speaking, Catholic, increasingly republican society inside the early United States, preserving much of its local culture at first but gradually experiencing stronger assimilationist pressure than it did in Canada. By the late nineteenth or twentieth century, it would probably still be recognizably French in language, memory, and religion, but less institutionally secure, less nationally central, and more like a powerful regional minority culture than a coequal national one.

human_answers: With this POD, Spain and, especially, France may have a very different trajectory from 1776. Both have been looking for a way to get back at Britain for the disastrous 7YW. ARW provided that way, OTL. That involvement did 2 things (more than that, but)...it waylaid the slow progress Spain was making up the Pacific Coast, and most importantly, helped set the stage for the French Revolution. There will be another war. Maybe the WoBavarian Succession spins out of control. Maybe Britain decides to assist Portugal in its struggles against Spain in mid-late 1770s, and this spins out of control. Maybe one or the other leaves the path to the French Revolution still on track. Or, maybe the wars are delayed, and FR as we know it is butterflied. That is beyond BIG. And, this all assumes that the colonies remain at peace, not rising up for round 2, or 3. During the Nootka Crisis, Spain looked to France for assistance, which it didn't get because of the FR. Plus, throughout the 18th century, France didn't go to Spain's aid, but, rather, expected it to be the other way around. I wouldn't count on France backing Spain in the Nootka Crisis, even if there was no FR. If left by its lonesome, Spain likely backs down as OTL. Or maybe Spain has used the decade or 2 of peace to continue settling the Pacific north coast.

I guess if England would have kept the economically important and more or less developed 13C it would have a smaller interest in Notka/Oregon/access to the pacific. If the ARW ends in 1775/1776 then yes, Spain would have had more time and resources to actually colonize Notka. To be honest, I never understood why so many people believe that with a failed ARW, the French R. simply never happens. France was still economically and politically and socially in a bad situation. So yeah, I think the FR still would have happened. Maybe sooner or later (most likely a bit later) and maybe less bloody, but IMO it still would have happened nonetheless. And yeah, France and Spain still would have tried to get revenge on England. How realistic is that if the ARW ends in 1775/1776? I mean the whole American mythos of Americans rising up against the british crown is not that true. A lot of American colonists were loyal to the crown. Its not that every peasant in the 13C rose up against George III and with that rebellion or uprising put down quickly, I think the motivation for another rebellion would be low. How realistic is a peaceful solution to the pacific question? So England keeps the 13C and let's say that that James Cook dies earlier so there is no English expedition at the pacific coast and England has less information and is less interested in these regions. And if Spain has more time, money to colonize Notka could England have decided to just let Spain have it?

If the United States had never come into existence, the British colonies in North America would probably have remained under British imperial administration at first, but they would not likely have stayed forever as tightly controlled colonies. The most plausible long-term outcome is that they would have evolved into something like Canada, Australia, or New Zealand: self-governing British dominions within the Empire, and eventually independent states or a federated North American dominion.

In the short term, administration would have continued through the British system already in place before independence. London governed through the Crown, the Board of Trade, colonial governors, and local assemblies. Each colony had its own charter, governor or lieutenant governor, courts, and elected assembly, but ultimate authority rested with Parliament and the Crown. Britain had already been trying after the Seven Years’ War to tighten imperial control, raise revenue, station troops, and regulate westward expansion. If no American break had occurred, this central oversight likely would have continued for some time, though Britain would probably have had to compromise more with colonial elites to keep the colonies stable.

Over time, the colonies would likely have gained more internal self-government. The British Empire in the nineteenth century increasingly shifted toward granting settler colonies control over domestic affairs while Britain retained authority over foreign policy, defense, and constitutional matters. In that scenario, the mainland colonies might have followed a path similar to British North America after 1776: provincial governments first, then perhaps regional unions, and eventually a larger federation. A single “British North America” stretching far beyond historical Canada is conceivable, though not guaranteed; regional divisions between New England, the Middle Colonies, the South, and the frontier might also have produced multiple dominions rather than one.

Slavery would have made administration especially complicated. Since Britain abolished slavery in most of its empire in the 1830s, a British North America that still included the southern mainland colonies would almost certainly have faced imperial emancipation. That could have caused major political conflict, perhaps even rebellion by slaveholding colonies, and might have led to some kind of restructuring or separation within British North America. So even if the USA never existed, the mainland colonies might not have remained one unified political unit.

Westward expansion would also have been different. Britain had tried to limit settlement beyond the Appalachians in 1763, partly to reduce conflict with Indigenous nations. Without an independent United States pushing aggressively westward as it did historically, expansion may have been slower, more negotiated, and more directly shaped by imperial strategy. But it would still probably have happened eventually, especially given settler population growth and imperial rivalry with Spain, France, and later Russia in North America.

By the late nineteenth or early twentieth century, the most likely administrative form would have been a dominion or a set of dominions under the British Crown, with responsible parliamentary government modeled on Westminster. In the very long run, these entities would probably have become fully sovereign, as Canada did, while perhaps retaining the monarch as head of state for some time.

So the simplest answer is: if the USA had never existed, Britain would probably not have ruled the North American colonies forever as old-style colonies. They would most likely have moved from crown-and-parliament administration, to self-governing dominions within the British Empire, and eventually to independence, either as one large federated British North American state or as several successor states.

items.question: What If the British won the 1812 War?
human_answers: As far as the political landscape is concerned, I think the Federalists are routed as per OTL. They'll be blamed for losing the war, even if theyre ultimately vindicated over the long haul about being right about how the war would go. The whole post-war love affair that existed OTL is going to be gone, and I think the eight years following the war are going to be politically toxic. Depending on the border shuffling, the US might lose multiple free states which will affect the long term sectional rivalry already in development. Illinois might flip to a slave state due to butterflies if the slavers back a single candidate upon the state's formation. The Virginian dynasty probably crumbles and Monroe probably stays put as Secretary of State instead of seeking the presidency. If the Battle of New Orleans doeant take place Jackson's path to power is much longer and more arduous, if he even seeks the office at all. Theres a not unreasonable chance that the capital moves to Philadelphia and stays there. America may seek to purchase Texas around the time they signed the Adams-Onis Treaty of OTL, they could afford it, and if Monroe is still Secretary of State they're probably dabbling more in that area as it was already a pet project of his. If Texas isn't purchased, I think there's going to be a greater push against annexation by the Whigs given the greater disparity between free and slave states. A lot depends on the peace treaty, though.

I would consider OTL to be a tie, and I think spin city can depict it as such at the time. I've seen threads arguing it was a USAmerican victory because Britain wasn't able to conquer them. What does winning look like? Typically, it means taking something from the loser. Since USA never gained anything during the war, there's nothing they can be forced to give back. So, it would have to be something they held prior (or had claim to). Retaking control of any of the lost colonies is largely devoid of reality. Border adjustments in Maine/Vermont/New York are on the table. Making the old Northwest part of Canada, perhaps as a Native Reserve, is a possibility. Would Britain keep New Orleans if they had taken it prior to truce and/or the rest of Louisiana? Give it back to Spain? Trade it for full control of the NW, if they haven't secured control of that already? Realistically, how much could Britain gain? But, I think OP wants to discuss political ramifications if the war ends with there being zero doubt which side won. There could be a major territorial concession which is bound to completely change the USA even if it rebounds spectacularly (such as loss of New Orleans/Louisiana), in which case political ramifications are a secondary concern. Or, territorial concessions are more limited, leaving things a bit more recognizable. A lot of things left unsettled by the ARW, are going to be settled in Britain's favor. Trade agreements may emerge also favoring Britain. Depending on the severity of the peace, politics will also be severely affected far beyond a 'USA lost, unequivocally, but otherwise everything is the same' . So, yeah, we need to know the scope of the peace. The OP needs to be fleshed out more.

If Britain had clearly “won” the War of 1812, the biggest immediate effect would probably have been a much weaker United States and a stronger British position in North America, but not the permanent destruction of the U.S. A British victory could have taken several forms—holding more American territory, forcing concessions in a peace treaty, strengthening Native buffer states in the Old Northwest, or humiliating the U.S. badly enough to change its politics for a generation.

The most likely major consequence would have been on the western frontier. One of Britain’s war aims, especially late in the conflict, was to support the creation of a Native American buffer state between the United States and Canada. If Britain had won decisively enough to impose terms, that idea might have survived. In that case, U.S. expansion into the Great Lakes and upper Midwest would have slowed dramatically. Figures like Tecumseh might have become even more historically central, and Native resistance to U.S. settlement would have had much stronger backing. This would not necessarily have stopped U.S. expansion forever, but it could have delayed it by decades and changed the map of the interior.

In Canada, a British victory would have strengthened loyalty to the empire and deepened the sense that British North America had successfully resisted U.S. invasion. Canadian identity already drew heavily from that experience; a clearer British triumph would have made that even stronger. The border might also have become more militarized and politically important much earlier.

Inside the United States, the political consequences could have been severe. The war was already controversial, especially in New England. A humiliating defeat might have discredited the “War Hawks” and the Republican leadership under Madison. The Federalists, instead of collapsing after the Hartford Convention, might have revived as the party of commercial stability and anti-war caution. American nationalism, which in actual history was energized by the war’s symbolic victories, might have developed more slowly and more defensively.

That matters because the War of 1812 helped create a story that the U.S. had fought Britain to a draw and earned international respect. If Britain had clearly won, that sense of national self-confidence would have been shaken. Mythic events like Andrew Jackson’s rise after New Orleans might never have had the same power. Jackson himself might not have become a national hero, which could have altered the future of American democracy, Indian removal, and party politics in the 1820s and 1830s.

Economically, a British victory might have kept the United States more vulnerable to British commercial pressure. The U.S. would still likely have grown, because its population and land resources were enormous, but its leaders might have been more cautious in challenging Britain at sea and in foreign trade. American industrialization, which got a boost from wartime disruption and postwar nationalism, may have proceeded more unevenly.

In foreign affairs, Britain would have emerged with greater prestige and leverage in North America, though probably not with a desire to reconquer the United States. By 1812–1815 Britain was more concerned with Napoleon and global strategy than with restoring the old colonies. So even in victory, Britain likely would have sought a stable, subordinate U.S., not annexation. The Monroe Doctrine, issued in 1823, might have been weaker, delayed, or less credible if the U.S. had recently suffered defeat by Britain.

In the long run, the U.S. probably still becomes a large and powerful country because of its demographics, resources, and distance from Europe. But a British victory could have produced a North America where Canada was more secure, Native confederacies remained stronger for longer, U.S. western expansion slowed, and American nationalism matured later and with less confidence. In short, Britain winning the War of 1812 would most likely not have erased the United States, but it could have made the 19th-century continent more British, more Indigenous in the interior for a time, and less decisively dominated by the U.S.
